one_liner: Firebolt's free self-hosted distributed SQL engine (ClickHouse-derived runtime); beats DuckDB on ClickBench hot runs, roughly ties ClickHouse.
what_it_does: A free, self-hosted edition of Firebolt's cloud data-warehouse query engine. It ships as one prebuilt Docker image (ghcr.io/firebolt-db/engine:dev) and runs on a single node or as a multi-node cluster (Docker Compose, or Kubernetes via Firebolt's Helm chart/operator docs). You use it as a server: SQL in a Postgres-compliant dialect with analytic extensions, sent over HTTP on port 3473, or through the fb CLI, JDBC, SQLAlchemy or a separate web-UI image. It queries Parquet and Iceberg on S3, GCS or local files directly, and ingests into its own indexed columnar tables.
how_it_is_fast: Per Firebolt's CDMS 2022 paper ('Assembling a Query Engine From Spare Parts'), the runtime is a hard fork of ClickHouse's vectorized execution engine. The planner, forked from HPI's Hyrise, does cost-based join reordering, and a custom shuffle-based distributed executor replaced ClickHouse's distributed layer so that large-large joins and high-cardinality GROUP BYs scale out. Managed tables are immutable tablets sorted on a PRIMARY INDEX, with a sparse index of one mark per 8,192-row granule (found by binary search), per-tablet min/max statistics, min/max data-skipping indexes, Roaring-bitmap inverted indexes and aggregating indexes, and the scan refines a selection vector one predicate at a time so wide columns are decoded only for rows that survive. I/O goes through io_uring, and tablets are cached on local SSD with prefetching; none of this can be checked in source, because only the binary is published.
when_to_use: Repeated, dashboard-style aggregations over one large fact table on a big-RAM machine where hot-cache latency matters: its ClickBench hot-run sum on c8g.metal-48xl is 2.66 s, vs 3.14 s for ClickHouse and 11.29 s for DuckDB.
Queries that filter or join on a sort key, where the sparse primary index, data-skipping, inverted and aggregating indexes can prune most granules before any column data is read.
You want one engine that runs as a single Docker container on a laptop and scales to a multi-node cluster with shuffle joins and distributed aggregations, all in a Postgres-style SQL dialect.
Ad-hoc SQL over Parquet or Iceberg in S3/GCS (or S3-compatible stores such as MinIO or R2) without a separate load pipeline.
Self-hosting inside your own product is acceptable under Elastic License 2.0, which bars only offering it as a competing hosted service.
when_not_to_use: Cold or first-touch latency matters: after a restart, each ClickBench query except Q1 took at least ~0.47 s (vs ~0.001 s minimum for ClickHouse and 0.04-0.09 s for DuckDB), which makes the cold geomean 1.6-2.3x slower than DuckDB's.

Machines with 32 GB of RAM or less under concurrent load. In ClickBench's 10-connection concurrency test, 30% (c6a.4xlarge) and 57% (c8g.4xlarge) of queries errored, vs 0.1% for ClickHouse. 18 of 43 queries returned no result on c6a.large (4 GB) and 7 on c6a.xlarge (8 GB). The README recommends at least 16 GB.
You need an embeddable in-process library (DuckDB, DataFusion), or you must build, audit, patch or vendor the engine: it is a closed binary under a non-OSI license.
Write-concurrent workloads: only one write transaction can be active per engine at a time, and a second concurrent write returns an error.

Networks you don't trust, or restricted hosts. The engine's HTTP endpoint has no built-in authentication or TLS, and a large-DDL bug (issue #59) left metadata unusable after the fix. It needs Linux 6.1+ io_uring, seccomp=unconfined and an 8 GiB memlock ulimit, and Docker Desktop for Mac 4.42.1-4.43.1 cannot run it.

integration.form: prebuilt server binary in a Docker image (ghcr.io/firebolt-db/engine); no library, headers or source
integration.dependencies: Docker Engine (plus the Compose plugin for multi-node); any HTTP client, or the fb CLI, JDBC or SQLAlchemy drivers; metadata is kept in SQLite on a single node and in PostgreSQL in cluster deployments
integration.min_toolchain: not applicable (no source). Host needs Linux kernel 6.1+ for io_uring, or Docker Desktop 4.43.2+ on macOS
integration.platforms: amd64 with at least SSE 4.2, or arm64 (multi-arch images); Linux host (macOS via Docker Desktop with socket-on-tmpfs workaround)
integration.thread_safety: Server process; any number of concurrent read transactions, but only one write transaction per engine at a time (concurrent writes error out)

gotchas: Errors come back as a JSON body with an 'errors' key, even with HTTP 200. During startup the port answers 'Cluster not yet healthy' at HTTP 200, so readiness checks must inspect the result body rather than the status code.

The response's statistics.elapsed understates query time by up to 3.6x on high-core machines, because the trailing statistics chunk is sent tens of milliseconds after the rows. ClickBench measures client wall-clock time for this reason.

ClickBench runs with enable_result_cache, enable_subresult_cache and enable_scan_cache set to false 'so timings are real'. Set these explicitly in your own benchmarks, or repeated queries may measure cache hits.

The HTTP protocol is stateless: the current database and explicit transactions are carried by echoing the Firebolt-Update-Parameters / Firebolt-Remove-Parameters response headers back as query-string parameters, so naive clients silently lose that state.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Apache DataFusion or Databend when you want a ready-made scale-out server with a Postgres dialect and index-driven pruning, and closed source is acceptable. Its c7a.metal-48xl hot-run sum (3.11 s, 2026-08-29) is about a third of the catalogued DataFusion (9.78 s) and Databend (9.91 s) figures for that machine, though from different run dates. Choose DataFusion if you need Apache-licensed code you can embed or modify, and note that Umbra and ClickHouse still lead it on the ClickBench Combined score.
verified_claims_summary: ClickBench's 43 queries, run on single AWS instances (c6a, c7a and Graviton4 c8g families) with the hits dataset ingested into a managed table (PRIMARY INDEX CounterID, EventDate, UserID, EventTime, WatchID) and result, subresult and scan caches disabled (2026-08-29 image engine:dev, compiler and flags undisclosed). Hot runs beat native DuckDB by about 1.6x (geomean) on c6a.4xlarge (hot sums 15.6 s vs 26.3 s; ClickHouse 18.0 s) and about 3-3.8x on metal-class machines. They roughly tie ClickHouse, while cold runs trail both, so the June 2025 '#1 on ClickBench' claim no longer holds.
status_note: Actively maintained by Firebolt (repo commits through 2026-08-13; engine releases labelled 'preview release candidate', default tag :dev). Free to self-host under Elastic License 2.0, but the GitHub repo holds only deployment scripts, examples and license notices; the engine is a closed binary you cannot build, patch or vendor.
